St. Photios the Great

Saints

St. Photios the Great

Photius · St. Photios of Constantinople

Period
Ninth century;891 in the OCA’s account
Region
Constantinople; Bulgaria
Titles / vocation
Hierarch · Father · Confessor
Commemoration
February 6

Introduction

St. Photios is remembered as a learned Patriarch of Constantinople, teacher and theologian. The OCA’s account places his ministry amid disputes over Ignatius, relations with Rome, Bulgaria and the Creed. His writings also preserve extensive evidence of ancient literature.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The received life describes his education and service as a state secretary before his rapid passage through the clerical ranks and election as patriarch. Its account of the ensuing controversy is explicitly an Orthodox ecclesiastical perspective.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Education and accession

The OCA names the future missionary Cyril and the young emperor Michael among his pupils, connecting his intellectual life with both the imperial court and the later Slavic mission.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Early teaching paragraph

Life and notable events

The OCA describes deposition in867, restoration following Ignatius’s death and the council of879, then a second deposition in886. Its account associates the council with the Creed and the opposition to adding filioque.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Depositions and879 council

Death and martyrdom

The same life dates his death to891 after his final removal and records burial at the monastery of Eremia. It remembers suffering and exile rather than an execution.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Closing life

Writings and legacy

The most important of the works of Photius is his renowned Bibliotheca or Myriobiblon (ed. I. Bekker, 1824–1825), a collection of extracts from and abridgments of 280 volumes of classical authors (usually cited as Codices), the originals of which are now to a great extent lost. The work is specially rich in extracts from historical writers. To Photius we are indebted for almost all we possess of Ctesias, Memnon, Conon, the lost books of Diodorus Siculus, and the lost writings of Arrian. Theology and ecclesiastical history are also very fully represented, but poetry and ancient philosophy are almost entirely ignored. It seems that he did not think it necessary to deal with those authors with whom every well-educated man would naturally be familiar. …

Historical1911 encyclopaedia discussion of Photius’s writings. Its editions, manuscript inventory and contemporary expressions such as “now” refer to1911; they are not a current bibliography.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · 1911 article, literary works: Bibliotheca

… His most important theological work is the Amphilochia, a collection of some 300 questions and answers on difficult points in Scripture, addressed to Amphilochius, archbishop of Cyzicus (ed. Sophocles Oeconomus, Athens, 1858). Other similar works are his treatise in four books against the Manichaeans and Paulicians, and his controversy with the Latins on the Procession of the Holy Spirit. His Epistles, political and private, addressed to high church and state dignitaries, are valuable for the light they throw upon the character and versatility of the writer (ed. J. Valettas, London, 1864). …
